title: Spurious CBC Results: Smear Before You Scare
summary: Recognise CBC illusions — EDTA pseudothrombocytopenia, platelet satellitism, giant platelets, nucleated red cells and rouleaux — and apply the smear review, citrate recollection, NRBC correction and absolute-count conversion.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 31 Hit 3 (EDTA pseudothrombocytopenia — the K₃/K₂-EDTA PCV part is not taught), Hit 5 (NRBC correction), Hit 15 (rouleaux vs agglutination), Hit 16 (giant platelets), Hit 20 (absolute counts) and Traps 1 and 5. Checked against Cattaneo 2025, Hebbar 2014, Jakšić 2026, Deyrup 2022 and Arora 2024. Prevalence taught as ~0.1% of counts (reviewer: 0.1–2%). Not taught: rouleaux dispersal in saline/warming (not verified).

objectives: Explain how analyzers identify platelets, red cells and white cells.
Recognise EDTA pseudothrombocytopenia, satellitism and giant platelets.
Correct the WBC for NRBCs and convert percentages to absolute counts.

scenes.title: A platelet count of 38 — and no bleeding
scenes.altText: An analyzer printout: platelets 38 × 10⁹/L, flagged. The patient has a cough and no bruising or bleeding. A transfusion request card appears. Question token: “Real thrombocytopenia — or a lab illusion?”

cues.text: A patient with a cough has a platelet count of thirty-eight. She has no bruises and no bleeding.
Someone asks for a platelet transfusion.
Before anyone treats a number, the lab has to ask: is this count real?

scenes.title: Normal: how an analyzer counts cells
scenes.altText: A stream of cells passes a counting aperture. Platelets are identified mainly by being small; red cells are larger; nucleated cells are counted in the white-cell channel. A size histogram builds with a small platelet peak and a big red-cell peak. Note: anything that changes size or clumps cells into one particle fools the count.

cues.text: An analyzer counts thousands of cells as they flow, one by one, past a sensor.
Platelets are recognised largely because they’re small. Red cells are bigger. Nucleated cells go into the white-cell count.
Size histograms show a small peak for platelets and a much larger one for red cells.
So anything that clumps cells together, changes their size, or adds unexpected nucleated cells can fool the count.

scenes.title: What changes: four classic illusions
scenes.altText: Panel 1, EDTA pseudothrombocytopenia (~0.1% of counts): antibodies cause platelets to clump in EDTA, or stick to neutrophils (satellitism); clumps are not counted as platelets. Panel 2, giant platelets: too large to be recognised as platelets — falsely low count. Panel 3, nucleated red cells: counted as white cells — corrected WBC = WBC × 100 ÷ (100 + NRBC per 100 WBC). Panel 4, rouleaux vs agglutination: rouleaux are coin-like stacks from raised fibrinogen/immunoglobulins; agglutination is irregular antibody clumping (e.g., cold agglutinins).

cues.text: Illusion one: EDTA pseudothrombocytopenia, in about one in a thousand counts. Antibodies make platelets clump in the EDTA tube, or stick around neutrophils. The analyzer doesn’t count the clumps as platelets.
Illusion two: giant platelets are too big to be recognised as platelets, so the count comes out falsely low.
Illusion three: nucleated red cells get counted as white cells. Correct it: multiply the white count by one hundred, and divide by one hundred plus the NRBCs per hundred white cells.

Illusion four: rouleaux — red cells stacked like coins, caused by raised fibrinogen or immunoglobulins — are not the same as agglutination, the irregular clumping caused by antibodies such as cold agglutinins.

scenes.title: In the lab: check before you report
scenes.altText: A workflow: 1) Flagged low platelets with no bleeding → review the blood smear for clumps, satellitism or giant platelets — the smear is indispensable. 2) Recollect in an alternative anticoagulant such as citrate and compare. 3) Report percentages as absolute counts: absolute = total WBC × (% ÷ 100); WBC 6.0 × 10⁹/L with 70% neutrophils → 4.2 × 10⁹/L. 4) In neonates with many NRBCs, analyzers can grossly overestimate the WBC — manual review corrects it.

cues.text: Step one: a flagged low platelet count in a patient who isn’t bleeding sends you to the blood smear. Clumps, satellitism or giant platelets are easy to see there.
Step two: recollect in another anticoagulant, such as citrate, and compare. A big difference points to an EDTA artefact.
Step three: report differentials as absolute counts. Multiply the total white count by the percentage. Six times seventy percent gives four point two neutrophils.
Step four: in newborns with huge numbers of nucleated red cells, analyzers can wildly overestimate the white count — manual smear review gives the corrected value.

props.title: ④ Neonates, many NRBCs
lines: Analyzer WBC can be far too high

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “Critically low automated platelets → transfuse” is crossed out → “Check the smear and a citrate recollection first.” Trap card: “Report the WBC as counted when NRBCs are present” is crossed out → “Correct for NRBCs.” Trap card: “Rouleaux on the smear = cold agglutinins” is crossed out → “Rouleaux = proteins; agglutination = antibodies.”

cues.text: Trap one: never transfuse a critically low automated platelet count in a patient who isn’t bleeding until the smear — and if needed a citrate sample — confirm it.
Trap two: when nucleated red cells are present, correct the white count before reporting it.
Trap three: rouleaux aren’t cold agglutinins. Coin stacks come from proteins; irregular clumps come from antibodies.

props.title: ✗ “Report the WBC as counted despite NRBCs.”

scenes.title: Smear before you scare
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Smear before you scare” — look at the slide before calling a critical count. Plus “clump, giant, nucleated, stacked” as the four illusions. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: smear before you scare. And four illusions to rule out: clumped, giant, nucleated, stacked.

Where it breaks: citrate samples can occasionally clump too; true thrombocytopenia can coexist with an artefact; analyzers differ in how they count giant platelets and NRBCs; and a bleeding patient may need treatment before the workup is done.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Low platelets, no bleeding → smear (clumps, satellitism, giants) → recollect in citrate”, “Corrected WBC = WBC × 100 ÷ (100 + NRBC) · absolute = WBC × % · rouleaux ≠ agglutination”.

cues.text: Before reporting a surprising count, look at the smear: rule out platelet clumps, giant platelets, nucleated red cells and rouleaux — and report absolute, corrected numbers.

props.label: Low PLT, no bleeding → smear → recollect in citrate
WBC × 100 ÷ (100 + NRBC) · absolute = WBC × % · rouleaux ≠ agglutination

explanation.what: Plain language: analyzers can be fooled; a quick look at the smear catches most illusions. Scientific terms: EDTA-dependent pseudothrombocytopenia (~0.1% of counts) from in-vitro platelet agglutination or satellitism (IgG bridging GPIIb-IIIa to leukocyte FcγRIII); giant platelets not recognised by size-based counters; NRBCs counted as leukocytes — corrected WBC = WBC × 100 ÷ (NRBC/100 WBC + 100); rouleaux from immunoglobulins and acute-phase proteins neutralising RBC surface charge.
explanation.why: Counters classify by size and signal; clumps, giant cells and nucleated red cells fall into the wrong channel.
explanation.measure: Smear review of anticoagulated blood is indispensable; recollect in citrate (or other anticoagulant) to confirm; absolute count = total WBC × fraction; manual review in neonates with massive NRBCs.
explanation.differs: Pseudothrombocytopenia (no bleeding, clumps on smear) vs true thrombocytopenia; rouleaux (coin stacks; proteins) vs agglutination (irregular clumps; antibodies).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: “transfuse this platelet count?”, NRBC correction calculation, absolute neutrophil count, rouleaux vs agglutination.

mnemonic.text: Smear before you scare — clumped, giant, nucleated, stacked.
mnemonic.explanation: Review the smear before calling a critical count; four classic illusions to exclude.
mnemonic.limitation: Citrate can clump too; true thrombocytopenia can coexist with artefact; bleeding patients may need treatment first.

analogyLimitations: Cells, histograms and clumps are schematic, not real morphology.
Cold-agglutinin effects on red-cell indices and lipaemia interference are not covered here.
takeaway: Before reporting a surprising count, look at the smear: rule out platelet clumps, giant platelets, nucleated red cells and rouleaux — and report absolute, corrected numbers.

questions.stem: An analyzer reports WBC 15.0 × 10⁹/L. The smear shows 25 NRBCs per 100 WBCs. What is the corrected WBC?

options.rationale: Incorrect. This multiplies instead of dividing by 1.25.
Incorrect. This subtracts 25% instead of using the formula.
Incorrect. NRBCs were counted as WBCs and must be corrected for.

questions.stem: A non-bleeding patient has an EDTA platelet count of 38 × 10⁹/L; the smear shows large platelet clumps. What is the best next step?

options.text: Recollect in citrate (or another anticoagulant) and recount

options.rationale: Incorrect. The count is likely artefactual.
Incorrect. Clumps must be investigated and reported.
Incorrect. Exclude the in-vitro artefact first.

questions.stem: WBC is 2.0 × 10⁹/L with 80% lymphocytes and 15% neutrophils. What is the absolute neutrophil count?

options.rationale: Correct. 2.0 × 0.15 = 0.3 × 10⁹/L — severe neutropenia hidden behind percentages.
Incorrect. A percentage is not a count.
Incorrect. That is the absolute lymphocyte count.

claims.text: EDTA pseudothrombocytopenia ~0.1%; clumps/satellitism; giant platelets missed; smear indispensable; alternative anticoagulant comparison.
Corrected WBC = WBC × 100 ÷ (100 + NRBC/100 WBC); extreme NRBC interference in neonates.
Rouleaux from immunoglobulins/acute-phase proteins; agglutination in cold-antibody AIHA.
Analyzers identify platelets largely by small size; nucleated cells counted in the WBC channel.
Rouleaux disperse with saline dilution or warming.

morphology.note: Clumps, cells and histograms are schematic, not real smear morphology.
